strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across two domains (speech and music continuation), which the authors claim is the first application of continuous autoregressive latent modeling to music; this extends prior TTS-only work (SALAD, DiTAR) meaningfully.

Well-designed comparisons: discrete baselines (RQ-Transformer with 32/16 RVQ, MusicGen variant) were retrained on the same data with the same backbone, making the quality/speed comparison fair and controlled.

Both automatic metrics (FAD, PPX, VERT, ViSQOL, ABX, MOSNet) and human evaluation studies (50 raters, MOS, Bayesian Elo with confidence intervals) are reported, with the evaluation protocols described in detail in the appendix.

Thorough ablation study (Tab. 5) showing each component (noise augmentation, short-context transformer, head batch multiplier) contributes measurably, including a configuration approximating MAR that clearly fails — this substantiates the central claim that plain MAR does not transfer to rich audio.

Practical efficiency results are compelling: one-step consistency head gives up to ~2x overall speedup over an RQ-Transformer baseline with better FAD and comparable-or-better human ratings, plus a useful analysis (Tab. 6) of the consistency vs. TrigFlow trade-off across inference step counts.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameter tables for VAE, backbone, heads, and training (Tab. 9-10), human study details, and stated sample availability.
Supplementary experiments on short-context window sensitivity and 3B backbone scaling provide evidence the approach is not brittle to hyperparameters and improves with scale.
weaknesses: Limited novelty at the component level: the paper is largely an assembly of known techniques — MAR (Li et al., 2024), noise injection from Pasini et al. (2024b), short-context conditioning akin to DiTAR, and sCM consistency training (Lu & Song, 2025). The genuinely new elements (Gaussian temperature heuristic, head batch multiplier) are modest and the temperature method is an empirical hack with a hand-waved theoretical sketch (the Jacobian term is acknowledged as intractable but simply dropped).

Evaluation is restricted to unconditioned/text-internal continuation; no text-to-speech or text-to-music conditional generation benchmarks, which limits comparability to the state of the art (MusicGen, AudioLDM, etc.) and weakens the significance claim for practical deployment. The 3s-prompt continuation setting is a fairly narrow task.

Some headline claims are stronger than the evidence: overall speedups are modest (×1.3 for speech, ×1.9-2.2 for music), and human Elo/quality differences versus the strongest baselines are small relative to confidence intervals in some cases (e.g., Enjoyment Elo 1857 ± 28 vs 1824 ± 29).
The scalability study (A.2) is a single extra data point; a proper scaling analysis is deferred to future work despite scaling claims in the abstract/introduction.

The consistency model's behavioral properties (mode dropping/averaging, diversity at 1 step) are not deeply analyzed; the diversity analysis in Sec. 5.3 is limited to speaker-similarity on 100 samples.

Abstract states CALM 'achieves higher quality at lower computational cost than their discrete counterpart,' but the discrete baselines use specific configurations (8-RVQ Mimi, 32/16-RVQ EnCodec) rather than the strongest known systems; the claim should be scoped accordingly.

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across two modalities (speech and music continuation), combining automatic metrics (FAD, PPX, VERT, ViSQOL, ABX) with human studies (MOS-style ratings and Bayesian Elo pairwise comparisons) that include confidence intervals and a clearly described protocol

Thorough ablation study (Tab. 5) that isolates the contribution of each component, including a configuration approximating the original MAR setup, which convincingly shows the vanilla MAR approach fails on full-length music

Well-motivated engineering contributions with practical value: the head batch multiplier and the noisy long-context / clean short-context decomposition are sensible solutions to real training and inference bottlenecks, and the TrigFlow-vs-consistency analysis (Tab. 6) is informative for practitioners
Hyperparameter tables for both models and VAEs (Tabs. 9-10) and a 3B backbone scalability check in the appendix improve reproducibility relative to many audio generation papers
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core architecture is a direct application of MAR (Li et al., 2024) with a consistency head replacing the diffusion head (following Lu & Song, 2025 and Hang et al., 2025), and the noise-injection idea is taken from Pasini et al. (2024b); the remaining contributions (short-context transformer, head batch multiplier) are incremental engineering rather than new modeling insights

The Gaussian temperature sampling is an ad hoc heuristic with a hand-wavy theoretical justification: the paper derives the change-of-variables formula, declares the Jacobian term 'untractable', and then empirically applies temperature only to the Gaussian input. There is no analysis of what distribution the resulting latents actually follow, and the claimed equivalence to 'variance 1/sqrt(tau)' is stated without derivation

Comparisons are only against baselines retrained by the authors (RQ-Transformer variants, MusicGen). No comparison to the closest related continuous-audio systems (SALAD, DiTAR, Pasini et al.) on shared benchmarks, making it hard to assess absolute progress; the claimed 'state-of-the-art' improvement is against internal baselines only

The speedup comparison conflates architectural asymmetry with methodological advantage: the music consistency head has 601M parameters versus 701M for the RQ-Transformer head, while the speech consistency head has only 10M versus 701M, so the ×12.3 sampler speedup partly reflects a much smaller head rather than the consistency formulation itself; a fairer iso-compute comparison is needed

The scalability study is thin: a single 3B run reported as one table in the appendix, no training-compute-matched scaling curves, and no statement of token/step budgets, weakening the claim that continuous modeling is the better scaling path

Some claims lack support or are inconsistent: the abstract claims 'higher quality at lower computational cost' yet the music 1-step CALM ranks below the TrigFlow variant on acoustic quality, and the meaningfulness gain over the text-conditioned RQ-Transformer is speculative ('could be due to...'); the music VAE lacks semantic distillation, acknowledged but unaddressed, which may confound generative quality comparisons

Generative quality is evaluated only on the continuation task at a fixed 3s prompt + 27s generation; no text-to-music, zero-shot TTS, or streaming evaluation despite the framing around lightweight, edge-device, real-time generation (RTF analysis exists but is limited to the music model)

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement: the fidelity-vs-compute trade-off of RVQ-based discrete audio LMs is a real limitation, and moving to continuous latents with a consistency head is a sensible and timely direction.

Strong and fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation across both speech and music continuation: automatic metrics (FAD, ViSQOL, SISNR, PPX, VERT, ABX, MOSNet), speed/RTF measurements, and human studies (acoustic quality MOS and Bayesian Bradley-Terry Elo with 95% CIs) with a clearly documented protocol (Appendix B).

Baselines are retrained on the same data with the same backbone (32/16-RVQ RQ-Transformer, MusicGen-Medium variant), making the quality/speed comparisons reasonably fair rather than comparing against stale external checkpoints.

Useful ablations (Tab. 5) that isolate the contribution of each component (noise augmentation, short-context transformer, head batch multiplier), including a configuration approximating MAR that clearly fails, which supports the paper's central claim that vanilla MAR-style modeling is insufficient for rich audio.

The consistency head delivers a large practical win: 1-step sampling reduces sampler time by ×12–×20, and Tab. 6 carefully characterizes the consistency vs. TrigFlow trade-off across step counts in the real-time regime.

Honest treatment of negative/neutral findings (e.g., noise injection alone causes audio fading on long music sequences; short-context transformer unnecessary for speech; TrigFlow best quality but impractical for streaming), and a preliminary 3B scaling check (Tab. 8).
weaknesses: Novelty is largely integrative: the architecture is MAR (Li et al., 2024) plus components from prior audio work — noise injection is from Pasini et al. (2024b), local-context conditioning mirrors DiTAR (Jia et al., 2025), the consistency head is Lu & Song (2025). The genuinely new pieces (short-context transformer, head batch multiplier, Gaussian temperature heuristic) are engineering-level contributions, and the temperature method is admittedly a heuristic without theoretical grounding (the Jacobian term is simply dropped).

Task scope is narrow: only unconditioned/text-implied continuation is evaluated. The speech model uses an inner monologue but no true text-to-speech or text-to-music conditioning benchmark is reported, which limits comparison to the broader TTS/music-generation literature and to external SOTA (e.g., SALAD, DiTAR results are cited but not compared).

All headline results are against internally retrained baselines; the claim of beating 'state-of-the-art discrete audio language models' would be strengthened by comparisons to published pretrained systems and standard community benchmarks.

Human evaluations are modest in size (50 raters × 10 samples, 50 examples per method), and some Elo/MOS gaps between CALM and the strongest baseline (e.g., 1857 vs 1847 for 1-step vs 32-RVQ music) are within confidence intervals, so a few superiority claims are weaker than stated.

Reproducibility is unclear: no code or model release is mentioned (the sample link in the abstract is empty), training uses 16–48 H100s on a private 400K-song subset, which is not fully reproducible for most labs.

The music VAE comparison (Tab. 3) shows the 32-dim VAE only matches the 4-RVQ EnCodec, and 96–128 dims are needed for high-fidelity audio, which partially undercuts the 'higher fidelity at lower cost' framing since latent dimensionality and bitrate trade-offs are not analyzed in the same terms as RVQ bitrates.

Minor issues: missing content in the abstract ('Samples are available at'), typos ('MOSNeT', 'payed'), and Sec. 5's claimed trade-off discussion of Tab. 4/TigerFlow naming inconsistencies that should be cleaned up.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: replacing discrete RVQ tokenization with continuous latent autoregressive modeling via a consistency head addresses a real trade-off (fidelity vs. compute) in audio language models, with convincing speedup evidence (up to ~19x sampler speedup, ~2.2x overall).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four tasks (speech continuation, TTS, music continuation, text-to-music) with both automatic metrics (FAD, PPX, VERT, WER/CER, ViSQOL, SISNR) and properly designed human studies (MOS, pairwise/Bayesian Elo, 50 raters, methodology detailed in Sec. G).

Fair comparisons: discrete RQ-Transformer baselines and MusicGen/EnCodec variants were retrained on the same data and backbones, not just quoted from other papers; an explicit ablation study (Tab. 5) isolates the contribution of noise augmentation, short-context transformer, and head batch multiplier.

Useful practical innovations beyond a straight MAR port: noise-injected long context plus clean short-context transformer, consistency (or LSD) heads for 1-step sampling, Gaussian temperature sampling, head batch multiplier, latent CFG, and latent distillation — each ablated or analyzed in appendices.

Significant practical impact: the released 100M-parameter Pocket TTS that runs faster than real-time on CPU, plus a strong TTS result (WER 1.81 on LibriSpeech test-clean) competitive with or better than F5-TTS, DiTAR, and SALAD baselines.

Honest treatment of weaknesses, e.g., the low WavLM speaker-similarity score traced back to the VAE, and follow-up human evaluation; appendix analyses of TrigFlow vs. consistency and scalability to a 3B backbone.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely architectural/engineering assembly: MAR-style backbone + consistency head + noise augmentation (Pasini et al.) + short-context conditioning (cf. DiTAR patching) + latent CFG (already in SoundReactor). Individual components are mostly known; the contribution is their combination and empirical validation in audio at scale.

Draft-quality artifacts undermine polish: a placeholder reference ('Placeholder Author... Replace with accurate reference if you have one'), a missing sample URL in the abstract, and truncated text in Section 1; the abstract's quality claim is not uniformly supported (e.g., TTS speaker similarity is below reference).

Sampler-head speedups (~x12–x20) overstate practical gains: overall end-to-end speedup is only ~1.3x (speech) to ~2.2x (music), and TrigFlow actually beats consistency on quality at higher step counts.

Some evaluation concerns: TTS comparisons to DiTAR/SALAD use paper-reported numbers on possibly different training data; music FAD computed on an internal test set; MusicCaps text-to-music comparison is secondary and the model was trained with CLAP audio-mode conditioning rather than captions; baselines in Tab. 12 were evaluated on Adobe-enhanced audio, which changes the protocol.

The speech model drops both noise injection and the short-context transformer, so the core 'CALM' architecture differs across tasks, making the unified-story framing slightly weaker; ablation is only thorough for music.

Claim of 'no complete scalability study' (left to future work) and music semantic distillation left open limit generality; no analysis of failure modes such as long-duration drift beyond brief mentions.

strengths: The paper is a comprehensive empirical study covering four tasks (speech continuation, TTS, music continuation, text-to-music) with consistent methodology across tasks, which is more thorough than most prior work on continuous autoregressive audio modeling (SALAD, DiTAR, MELLE are TTS-only).

The ablation study (Tab. 5) is well-designed and informative: it isolates the contribution of noise augmentation, the short-context transformer, and the head batch multiplier, and shows that the plain MAR configuration fails badly (FAD 8.38), substantiating the paper's central claim that vanilla continuous autoregression does not transfer to music.

Extensive evaluation protocol: objective metrics (FAD, PPX, VERT, WER/CER), human studies with 50 raters and a fully specified Bayesian Elo methodology (Sec. G), a scalability probe with a 3B backbone, and an inference-speed/quality tradeoff analysis (Tab. 9) that fairly motivates the consistency head over TrigFlow in the streaming regime.
The Pocket TTS release (100M params, faster than real-time on laptop CPU, lowest WER on LibriSpeech test-clean among compared systems) is a concrete, verifiable artifact with practical value.
The writing is generally clear, the background section is pedagogically solid, and hyperparameters (Tab. 13-14) are reported at unusual depth, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. Each component is imported from prior work: the MAR backbone (Li et al., 2024), noise injection (Pasini et al., 2024b), consistency/TrigFlow heads (Lu & Song, 2025), shortcut-style few-step heads (Hang et al., 2025), latent CFG (explicitly credited to SoundReactor, Saito et al., 2025), and DiTAR already showed the value of local patch context. The genuinely new pieces (Gaussian temperature heuristic, head batch multiplier, latent distillation) are engineering-level contributions. The paper is best viewed as a careful integration/scaling study rather than a new method.

The headline claim of 'higher quality at lower computational cost' is weaker than presented. The music VAE requires 96-128 latent dimensions (Tab. 7) to match the 32-RVQ codec, and CALM's FAD advantage over the same-backbone RQ-Transformer baseline is modest (0.83 vs 1.06 at 1 step; the 4-step model only reaches 0.71), while the TrigFlow variant that achieves the best quality is 3x slower than baseline - a result that sits awkwardly with the efficiency narrative.

Comparison fairness is questionable in places. Several TTS baselines are closed-source and results are copied from their papers (DiTAR, SALAD) under potentially different training data and protocols; the music baselines are internal retrainings; text-to-music evaluation on the MusicCaps benchmark uses an internal test set for training-time comparisons; and the speaker-similarity result (SIM 0.52 vs reference 0.69) is a substantial quality gap explained away via a VAE round-trip argument and a human study whose conclusion (all methods beat ground truth on speaker similarity) is surprising and not deeply investigated.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top venue: a placeholder bibliography entry ('Replace with accurate reference if you have one'), incomplete sentences with missing URLs in the abstract and Sec. F ('Samples are available at', 'the following technical report:'), a broken/empty figure layout in Sec. H, and an apparent duplicate ranking in Tab. 6 where both the RQ-Transformer and CALM are listed as rank 1 despite different Elo values. These suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

Some important details are underspecified or internally inconsistent: the paper claims consistency sampling with 'only one step', yet the best music results use 4 steps; the TTS model reportedly gains nothing from noise injection or the short-context transformer, which fragments the unified story; and the speech continuation speedup is only x1.3 overall, well below the x12.3 sampler-head figure emphasized in the abstract.

The claim that latent CFG and latent distillation are contributions is overstated - the paper itself notes latent CFG was introduced in SoundReactor, and the distillation is a straightforward L2 feature distillation of a CFG-conditioned teacher.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: the quality/compute trade-off imposed by RVQ tokenization in audio language models. Moving to continuous latents with a 1-step consistency head is a well-motivated and practically impactful direction.

Comprehensive experimental coverage across four tasks (speech continuation, TTS, music continuation, text-to-music), with both automatic metrics (FAD, WER/CER, PPX, VERT, PESQ, STOI, MOSNet, ViSQOL) and carefully described human evaluations (MUSHRA-style and Bayesian Elo with Bradley-Terry details in Appendix G).

The ablation study (Table 5) is convincing: it isolates the contributions of noise augmentation, the short-context transformer, and the head batch multiplier, and shows that a vanilla MAR-style configuration fails on full-length music, which directly supports the paper's central claims.

Baselines are fairly constructed: the discrete RQ-Transformer baselines use the same backbone and were retrained on the same data, which strengthens the continuous-vs-discrete comparison. The scalability check (3B vs 1.35B backbone, Table 10) and TrigFlow vs consistency comparison (Table 9) add valuable insight.

The combination of techniques is well-engineered, and the released Pocket TTS (100M params, faster than real-time on laptop CPU) demonstrates real practical value and provides a concrete artifact for the community.
Detailed appendices with full hyperparameters (Tables 13-14), data composition, and evaluation methodology support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely incremental. The core architecture is MAR (Li et al., 2024) applied to audio; noise injection follows Pasini et al. (2024b); the short-context transformer echoes DiTAR's patching observation; latent CFG is adopted from SoundReactor; consistency/trigflow heads and distillation are existing techniques. The paper is best viewed as a strong systems/engineering integration rather than a fundamentally new method.

There are noticeable polish and consistency issues that should have been caught: a placeholder bibliography entry ('Replace with accurate reference if you have one'), broken/missing links for samples and the Pocket TTS blog post in the abstract and Appendix F, typos ('too small enough', 'payed'), and occasional inconsistencies (e.g., 'We keep the value of 8' immediately after discussing 4-step evaluations). These raise concerns about the maturity of the submission.

The TTS speaker similarity results are weak and only partially explained: CALM scores 0.52, below F5-TTS (0.66) and DSM (0.67), and the VAE itself degrades similarity (0.57 vs 0.69 reference). The human evaluation claiming 'all measured methods beat the ground truth' is surprising and under-analyzed; the authors offer conjecture rather than a convincing diagnosis.

Some comparisons rely on paper-reported numbers for closed-source baselines (DiTAR, SALAD) whose training data and conditions differ from the authors' 88k-hour setup, weakening the fairness of Table 3.

The music/text-to-music evaluations are primarily on an internal test set; the MusicCaps benchmark (Table 11) shows CALM trailing on CLAP score (0.44 vs MusicFlow's 0.52) and the setup differs from baselines not retrained on the same data.
The Gaussian temperature sampling heuristic is ad hoc, with no theoretical grounding, and its discussion is thin given how much it affects the headline speech results (Table 2).
Reproducibility is promised but not yet demonstrated: code release is future tense, and the model/sample links are absent at submission time.
